ConflictOut.description:
One conflict the user must answer.

`actions` is the closed set of three choices for this conflict's kind. `dismiss` is not
among them and cannot be expressed.
ConflictOut.title: ConflictOut

ConflictResolutionIn.description:
The body of a resolution: which of the three, and which event is the new one.

`new_side_id` is required because the pair row is **symmetric** — it stores both sides
sorted, so the row cannot say which side the user just created. The prompt's asymmetry
lives in the client (it knows which event it just made) and comes back here.

The body carries the id only, not the kind: this endpoint resolves conflicts *on
personal events*, so the new side is a personal event by definition. That keeps the
shape narrow — a client cannot name a saved event's id and have it deleted.
ConflictResolutionIn.title: ConflictResolutionIn

ConflictResolutionOut.description:
The outcome of a resolution.

`new_side_id` is the event the prompt called "new" — the client opens it in edit mode
for `edit_new`, or finds it already deleted for `delete_new`.
ConflictResolutionOut.title: ConflictResolutionOut

ConflictSideOut.description:
One side of a conflict: the event that clashes.

The times are UTC instants. The side does not carry a timezone of its own — the sides
are two records that may live in two different zones, and a conflict is about the
instants they occupy, not about how either is displayed.
ConflictSideOut.title: ConflictSideOut

CsrfTokenOut.description:
The CSRF token the frontend sends back on every unsafe request.

The token is also set as the `csrftoken` cookie on the same response; the frontend
reads the cookie and echoes the value in the `X-CSRFToken` header. Sending both is
Django's own convention, and it is the one `CsrfViewMiddleware` checks.
CsrfTokenOut.title: CsrfTokenOut

CurrentUserOut.description:
The signed-in user.

The id and the email are what the frontend needs. There is no password field, no
permission field and no catch-all, so nothing internal can ride along.

The onboarding status is **not** here yet: `personalization` owns onboarding progress,
and it does not exist yet. It is added when it does, through `personalization`'s
published interface — this item does not depend on that one.
CurrentUserOut.title: CurrentUserOut

EventListOut.description: One page of the public catalog, and what the frontend needs to page through it.
EventListOut.title: EventListOut

EventOut.description:
One public event.

`id` is the stable identifier the API is keyed by; `slug` is the public page route's
key (the spine's Ids convention: a page URL uses the slug, never the PK).
EventOut.title: EventOut

EventPage.description:
The list endpoint's query parameters.

`city` matches the venue's city exactly, case-insensitively. The date bounds are
inclusive and apply to the start time.
EventPage.title: EventPage

HealthUnavailableOut.description: The shared error shape, with the per-component details typed for the client.
HealthUnavailableOut.title: HealthUnavailableOut

PasswordResetConfirmIn.description: The reset confirmation: the token from the reset link, and the new password.
PasswordResetConfirmIn.title: PasswordResetConfirmIn

PasswordResetConfirmOut.description:
The reset-confirmation answer.

The password has been changed and the account's other sessions have ended.
PasswordResetConfirmOut.title: PasswordResetConfirmOut

PasswordResetRequestIn.description: The reset request: the address to reset.
PasswordResetRequestIn.title: PasswordResetRequestIn

PasswordResetRequestOut.description:
The reset-request answer. The same for a known address and an unknown one.

It says the request was received, and nothing about whether there is an account.
PasswordResetRequestOut.title: PasswordResetRequestOut

PersonalEventCreateIn.description:
The body of a create.

The IANA timezone is **required**: a floating local time is refused rather than guessed,
because the user's wall clock and the event's zone are not the same thing.
PersonalEventCreateIn.title: PersonalEventCreateIn

PersonalEventListOut.description: The user's own personal events, soonest first.
PersonalEventListOut.title: PersonalEventListOut

PersonalEventListQuery.description:
The query parameters of the list endpoint.

This is a **separate** schema from `PersonalEventListOut`, and it has to be. A
schema-typed argument is a request *body* unless it is wrapped in `Query(...)`; and the
response schema has no bounds on it, so using it as the query model would silently
accept `?starts_after=…` and then ignore it.

The bounds are inclusive and apply to the start time. Both are optional: with neither,
the list is every event the user has.
PersonalEventListQuery.title: PersonalEventListQuery

PersonalEventOut.description:
One personal event.

`version` rises by one on every edit (AD-7's send key uses it, so it may only go up).
PersonalEventOut.title: PersonalEventOut

PersonalEventPatchIn.description:
The body of an edit. Every field is optional — an edit changes only what it names.

A field left out is unchanged. There is no way to *clear* `location` or `notes` through
this shape, because `None` and "not mentioned" are the same value here; that is a
deliberate limitation of a first-cut edit endpoint, not an oversight.
PersonalEventPatchIn.title: PersonalEventPatchIn

SavedEventListOut.description:
The user's saved events, and how many were left out.

`omitted` counts the saves whose catalog event has since disappeared — superseded or
unpublished. They are not listed, because they have no title to show, but they are not
hidden either: the count lets the client tell the user that something they saved is no
longer available, rather than silently dropping it.
SavedEventListOut.title: SavedEventListOut

SavedEventListQuery.description:
The query parameters of the saved-events list endpoint.

The bounds are inclusive and apply to the **snapshot's** start time — the same value the
list returns — so a filtered item and its own timestamp never disagree (AD-21).
SavedEventListQuery.title: SavedEventListQuery

SavedEventOut.description:
One saved public event.

**The times come from the snapshot; the display fields come from the catalog.** They
are two different places, and keeping them straight is the point (AD-21):

- `start_time_utc` and `end_time_utc` are the **snapshot** — what the user saw when
  they saved, updated only by AD-17 propagation.
- `title`, `venue_name` and `canonical_url` are the **catalog's current** values, read
  at request time. An editorial correction shows up immediately.

`event_version` is the snapshot's version of the catalog event. It is what lets the
system detect that the snapshot is behind, and it is what `stale` is measured against.
SavedEventOut.title: SavedEventOut

SchedulingConflictDetails.description: The `details` of a 409: which event was written, and what it clashes with.
SchedulingConflictDetails.title: SchedulingConflictDetails

SchedulingConflictOut.description:
The 409 a conflicting create or edit answers with.

It is an `ErrorOut` — `{code, message, details?}` — with the `details` field
**narrowed** to the conflict payload. That narrowing is the point: the client has to
render the three actions (FR-58), so the shape of the conflict has to be in the
generated contract, not just in the prose of the description. With the plain `ErrorOut`
the `details` would be an untyped dictionary, and a client generated from the OpenAPI
document could not read a single field of it.

The message and code come from `domain.errors.SchedulingConflictError`; the API layer
builds the body, so the two stay in step through this schema.
SchedulingConflictOut.title: SchedulingConflictOut

SignInIn.description: The sign-in request: an address and a password.
SignInIn.title: SignInIn

SignInOut.description:
The sign-in answer. The same for a wrong password and an unknown address.

The status is the only field. A body that named the account, or said which half of
the pair was wrong, would be the enumeration leak the services are careful to avoid.
SignInOut.title: SignInOut

SignOutOut.description: The sign-out answer. The session is over; nothing else is said.
SignOutOut.title: SignOutOut

SignUpIn.description:
The sign-up request: an address and a password.

The password is a plain string here and is never echoed back. It goes to
`apps.identity.services.sign_up`, which validates it against Django's configured
password validators and hashes it.
SignUpIn.title: SignUpIn

SignUpOut.description:
The sign-up answer. The same for a new address and an existing one.

There is no `created` flag, and no account id: either would say whether the address
was taken. The account holder of an existing address is told by email instead.
SignUpOut.title: SignUpOut

get.description: The CSRF token the frontend sends back on every state-changing request, in the `X-CSRFToken` header. The token is also set as the `csrftoken` cookie on this response, so the frontend can read it from there. This is a safe request, so it is not itself checked for a token.
The signed-in user's id and email. An anonymous request is refused with 401. Nothing internal is returned: there is no password hash, no permission list and no catch-all field.

post.description: Asks for a reset link. A known address gets one, by transactional email; an unknown address gets nothing. The answer is the same either way, so the endpoint cannot be used to find out who has an account.

Consumes a reset token and sets a new password. The token is single-use and short-lived: a token that was already used, revoked or expired is refused, and the refusal does not say which of the three it was. The account's other sessions end, so a stolen session does not survive the password change.

Authenticates an email and a password and establishes the session. A wrong password and an unknown address are answered identically — the same status and the same body — so neither can be used to find out who has an account.
Ends the session the request carries. The session cookie is cleared, so the next request is anonymous.

Creates an account and signs the user in. The answer is the same whether the address was new or already taken: an existing account holder is told by email instead. A caller who signs up with an address that is already taken, and who does not know that account's password, is not signed in.

get.description: Published, non-superseded events that have not started yet, soonest first. Optional city and date-range filters. No session is used and none is set.
One published event by id. An event that is not public — or that has already started — reads as not found, the same set the list shows. No session is used and none is set.
The user's own personal events, soonest first. No one else's are listed.
get.summary: List the signed-in user's personal events

post.description: Creates a personal event. The IANA timezone is required — a floating local time is refused rather than guessed. If the new event clashes with one already on the calendar, the response is 409 carrying the conflict and the three actions; the client then posts one of them to the resolve endpoint.

Records the user's choice on a conflict prompt. Exactly one of the three actions the prompt offered is accepted; there is no dismiss. A resolution that is illegal for this conflict's kind is refused, and the prompt stays open.

delete.description: Removes one of the signed-in user's personal events.

get.description: One of the signed-in user's personal events. An event that is not theirs reads as not found.

patch.description: Edits a personal event and re-runs conflict detection. A conflicting edit returns the same 409 payload a conflicting create does.

get.description: The user's own saved events, soonest first. The times are the snapshots — what the user saw when they saved — and the titles and venues are the catalog's current values. `omitted` counts the saves whose catalog event has since disappeared; they are not listed, but they are not hidden either.
get.summary: List the signed-in user's saved events

delete.description: Removes one of the signed-in user's saves. The conflict pairs it took part in close as `cleared_by_state_change` — the pair ended because a side went away, which is not a user resolution.

post.description: Saves a public catalog event onto the signed-in user's own calendar. The save is idempotent: saving an event that is already saved returns the existing record. The times in the response are the snapshot taken at save time; `stale` says whether the catalog has moved past it, in which case re-propagation has been requested. If the save clashes with a personal event, the response is 409 carrying the conflict and the three actions.
